Overtaken
o-ver-ta'kn
pp. (caught up with; come upon suddenly; and of sin, surprised into a fault)
From over and take. The picture is of something faster catching a man from behind — a pursuer, a storm, or a temptation that arrives before he has seen it coming.

Biblical Definition

The word appears twice and describes two kinds of pursuit. David of his enemies: “I have pursued mine enemies, and overtaken them: neither did I turn again till they were consumed” (Psa 18:37) — the deliberate, successful chase of a warrior king. Paul of a brother: “Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). This is one of the most carefully worded sentences in the New Testament and every clause is load-bearing. The man is overtaken — caught, surprised, not a settled rebel. The ones who act are ye which are spiritual, not the offended or the eager. The verb is restore, a word used of setting a broken bone and of mending nets. The manner is the spirit of meekness. And the safeguard is self-directed: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. Then the next verse names the whole operation: “Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2). Restoration is not leniency; it is the setting of a bone, which hurts and is meant to heal.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines overtake as to come up with in a course, pursuit or motion; to catch; and to come upon; to take by surprise.

expand to see more

OVERTA'KE, v.t.

1. To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress or motion; to catch.

He pursued his enemies and overtook them.

2. To come upon; to fall on afterwards.

3. To take by surprise. If a man be overtaken in a fault, ye who are spiritual, restore such an one. Gal. 6.

Key Scripture

Galatians 6:1 — "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."

Galatians 6:2 — "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

Psalm 18:37 — "I have pursued mine enemies, and overtaken them: neither did I turn again till they were consumed."

1 Corinthians 10:13 — "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it."

Modern Corruption

Galatians 6:1 is either ignored, so that the fallen are discarded, or amputated at the word restore, so that no fault is ever named.

expand to see more

The commonest failure is simple abandonment. A believer is overtaken, the matter becomes known, and the congregation's instinct is distance — not from doctrine but from embarrassment. Galatians 6:1 gives a command with an assigned party: ye which are spiritual. That is not a compliment to the willing; it is a qualification, and it means the work belongs to mature men who can be trusted with a broken bone. Where nobody accepts the assignment, the fallen man is left to set the fracture himself, which is why so many never walk right again.

The opposite error takes the word restore and drops everything around it, producing a ministry in which nothing is ever named as a fault and restoration means a swift return to public standing. Paul's sentence does not permit that either. It calls the thing a fault, it requires the spirit of meekness rather than warmth, and it attaches a warning to the restorer: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. The whole procedure assumes the man doing the mending is capable of the same fall, which is exactly what 1 Corinthians 10:13 says of every temptation — it is common to man. There are no specialists in immunity, only brothers with bone-setting work to do.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek prolambano (G4301), to take beforehand, to surprise; katartizo (G2675), to mend, set a bone, restore; prautes (G4240), meekness.

expand to see more

Greek prolemphthe (G4301) — be caught beforehand, surprised; Galatians 6:1, the man overtaken rather than settled in sin.

Greek katartizete (G2675) — mend, repair, set in joint; the word used of mending nets in Matthew 4:21.

Greek en pneumati prautetos (G4240) — in a spirit of meekness; the required manner, not an optional tone.

Greek skopon seauton (G4648) — watching yourself; the restorer's own guard, in the singular amid plurals.

Greek anthropinos (G442) — such as belongs to man; 1 Corinthians 10:13, no temptation is exotic.

Usage

"“If a man be overtaken in a fault” — caught from behind, not entrenched."

"“Restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” — the word is used of setting a bone."

"“Considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” — no specialists in immunity."
